question: When the Euclidean distance in harmonic/HarMax prototype classification is replaced by cosine, Lp, Bray-Curtis, Canberra, Chebyshev, Hamming, or Mahalanobis geometry, which choices improve predictive performance, representation structure, optimization, and measured carbon cost across vision and language models—and do the theory, implementation, statistics, and reported emissions actually support the claimed three-way advantage?

key_findings.claim: The authors define a broad distance-tailored prototype-head design space, but the paper gives two non-equivalent descriptions of the objective, leaving unclear whether all experiments implement harmonic probabilities or ordinary softmax over negative distances.
key_findings.evidence: The main definition is p(k|x)=d_k^{-n}/sum_j d_j^{-n}, equivalent to logits -n log d_k. Appendix B describes a softmin/log_softmax implementation, and Appendix C instead says the head returns z=-D (or log similarity) followed by standard cross-entropy. Softmax(-D) is not HarMax except under a different link, and the shared configuration fixes n=1 without explaining how n enters the negative-distance implementation. This ambiguity is material because optimization, scale behavior, and all comparisons depend on the link as well as the metric.

key_findings.claim: Cosine harmonic heads produce large, useful gains on some deep convolutional settings, especially CIFAR-10/100 ResNet-50, but this is an architecture-specific result rather than uniform dominance.
key_findings.evidence: On CIFAR-100 ResNet-50, stable cosine reports accuracy 0.7381 versus 0.7006 for cross-entropy and 0.7047 for Euclidean harmonic, while emissions are 79.2831 versus 89.64 gCO2eq and PCA@90 falls from 50 to 8. On CIFAR-10 ResNet-50, stable cosine reports 0.9262 versus 0.8430 for cross-entropy and 0.9185 for Euclidean, emissions 40.6776 versus 48.65, and PCA@90=5 versus 50. These are the paper's strongest quantitative cases and support cosine as a promising ResNet choice under the reported recipe.

key_findings.claim: Several hard vision settings directly contradict the paper's broad accuracy language: harmonic heads can trail cross-entropy badly on shallow backbones and on PVT.
key_findings.evidence: For CIFAR-100 CNN, cross-entropy accuracy is 0.3795, whereas Bray-Curtis(normalized), unstable cosine, stable cosine, and Euclidean report 0.3229, 0.2602, 0.2501, and 0.2413; the cosine runs also emit 21-80% more CO2 than the 1.18 g baseline. For CIFAR-100 MLP, cross-entropy is 0.2617 versus 0.2260 for the best listed harmonic head and 0.1190 for Euclidean. For CIFAR-100 PVT, focal loss reaches 0.4017 and cross-entropy 0.3994, while Euclidean harmonic is 0.2864. Thus metric choice can partially repair a weak Euclidean head without making the harmonic family competitive with cross-entropy.

key_findings.claim: The aggregate accuracy test provides no multiplicity-corrected evidence that any non-Euclidean metric beats Euclidean harmonic loss, despite prose claiming robust or general dominance.
key_findings.evidence: Across 16 paired dataset-backbone settings, median improvements for normalized Bray-Curtis and stable/unstable cosine are +0.5317, +0.1598, and +0.0965, with raw p=0.17060, 0.45339, and 0.55208. Many other metrics have large negative medians. The table's 'Sig.' column marks raw p<0.05, yet every displayed adjusted p-value is above 0.05 (minimum 0.0736), so none survives the paper's own correction column. Appendix E itself concedes that non-Euclidean losses do not uniformly dominate Euclidean accuracy.

key_findings.claim: The PCA statistics show that distance choice changes variance concentration, but the direction and inferential status of the claimed interpretability improvement are internally inconsistent.
key_findings.evidence: Table 10 says its outcome is the number of PCs needed for 90% variance and that more-negative differences mean fewer components, yet the prose calls positive medians such as +12.8333 for normalized Bray-Curtis and +5.8333 for unstable cosine interpretability gains. The table labels several raw p-values significant while all adjusted p-values are 0.0988 or larger. Moreover, low PCA dimension or high top-PC variance can equally signal representational collapse; no semantic labels, human evaluation, causal probe, calibration, or prototype-faithfulness test establishes interpretability.

anchors.section: Appendix L.4, PCA as a first-pass tool

key_findings.claim: Headline language-model sustainability claims are not supported by the only explicit per-step emissions audit: every tested distance raises per-1k-step emissions relative to cross-entropy.
key_findings.evidence: The main text says cross-entropy usually has the largest emissions wedge and that cosine/Minkowski can be greener. Appendix L.3 reverses the per-step conclusion: all tested distances increase emissions on BERT, GPT, and Qwen; cosine adds the least, while Mahalanobis and Minkowski add the most. It then says net savings remain possible only if a head needs fewer steps, but the paper provides no numerical energy-to-target table demonstrating that offset. The final head is lightweight relative to the backbone in FLOP accounting, so any cumulative advantage would have to come from duration/convergence, not a cheaper head operation.

key_findings.claim: The vision emissions evidence is mixed and contains unresolved sign and aggregation inconsistencies, so only configuration-level measurements should be reused.
key_findings.evidence: Table 11 defines negative differences as greener and reports stable cosine median -0.0239 with p=0.97937; all adjusted p-values exceed 0.05. Page 43 describes 650.49 g over 680 runs and a roughly +/-8% band, then separately says Figure 7 totals 181.2 g over 12 combinations. Page 44 calls Mahalanobis(Standard)'s largest positive delta 'lower emissions,' while the plot axis is total emissions difference and surrounding sections elsewhere call that variant costly. Individual tables also show large reversals: MarathiSign PVT unstable cosine emits 7.3447 versus 2.85 g (+157.9%), and ResNet stable cosine 54.8139 versus 35.41 g (+54.8%).

anchors.section: Appendix G.4, Figure 7 and sign interpretation

key_findings.claim: The reported language-model optimization evidence is qualitative and does not establish the broad claim that cosine improves perplexity across GPT, BERT, Qwen, and GPT-2B.
key_findings.evidence: Radar plots are normalized relative to Euclidean and do not expose absolute values. The convergence appendix states that BERT-0.1B benefits, that GPT-0.1B harmonic heads reach accuracy earlier, and that GPT-2B/Qwen track cross-entropy closely; Figure 9 compares only cross-entropy, Euclidean, and Minkowski p=2 rather than the headline cosine head. No multi-seed numeric perplexity table, uncertainty, token budget, or downstream evaluation is provided for the language runs.

key_findings.claim: The modulo-addition study reports a broad positive result—most distance-tailored harmonic variants avoid delayed generalization and recover a near-circular two-dimensional representation—but it is a visual single-task replication without numerical grokking times or uncertainty.
key_findings.evidence: Cross-entropy train accuracy rises long before test accuracy and its first two PCs explain roughly 20-30%, while Euclidean and many non-Euclidean harmonic heads are described as reaching train/test accuracy together with explained variance near 100%. The appendix supplies plots rather than a table of steps-to-generalization, seeds, exact final accuracy, or failures, and attributes the circle to the loss without representation-matched controls.

anchors.section: Appendix I, Grokking analysis: Modulo Addition

key_findings.claim: The finite-minimizer and PAC-Bayes appendix does not prove the strong generalization story stated in the paper.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem A.2 establishes invariance only when both data representations x and prototypes W are jointly scaled, but its optimization setup treats x as given and optimizes W; restricting W alone to a unit sphere therefore does not follow from the stated invariance. The inverse-distance link is singular at d=0 unless the implementation's epsilon clamp is included. Theorem A.4 invokes a 'standard PAC-Bayes margin bound' with an unspecified compatible capacity norm but supplies no prior, posterior, KL term, perturbation construction, or conditions connecting finite norm to a nonvacuous bound. These arguments are best treated as sketches, not formal guarantees of tight generalization.

anchors.section: Appendix A.2, Theorem A.4 and Equations 3-5

key_findings.claim: The alternative-loss comparison narrows the contribution to a selectable trade-off, not a generally superior loss family.
key_findings.evidence: The paper evaluates focal loss, label smoothing, center loss, confidence penalty, and ArcFace. Focal and confidence-penalty variants slightly beat cross-entropy on CIFAR-100 PVT while Euclidean harmonic loses 28.3%; ArcFace reaches 0.9997 on MarathiSign PVT versus 0.9991 for the listed unstable cosine; confidence penalty is much greener than stable cosine on MarathiSign ResNet. Harmonic cosine is excellent on CIFAR ResNet, but the winning method changes by backbone, dataset, and objective.

anchors.section: Appendix G, ArcFace and fine-grained comparison

method.core_idea: Replace the Euclidean prototype distance in a harmonic classification/language-model head with a registry of non-Euclidean distances, then compare each geometry along predictive, representation-concentration, and energy/emissions axes while holding the backbone and most training settings fixed.
method.mechanism: A learned prototype w_k is assigned to every image class or vocabulary item. Given a hidden representation h, the intended harmonic formulation computes inverse-distance probabilities d(h,w_k)^(-n) normalized across prototypes; the implementation appendix also describes ordinary softmax logits -D(h,w_k), an unresolved difference. Distances include L1/L2/Lp/L-infinity, cosine, Canberra, Bray-Curtis, relaxed Hamming, and Mahalanobis variants. Vision experiments train MLP, CNN, ResNet-50, and PVTv2-B0 on five datasets; language experiments train GPT-0.1B, BERT-0.1B, Qwen2-0.5B, and GPT-2B on OpenWebText for 10,000 iterations. Evaluation combines accuracy/F1 or perplexity, gradient-norm variance, covariance effective rank, PCA concentration, CodeCarbon emissions, convergence plots, and a modulo-addition grokking case study. Wilcoxon paired tests aggregate 16 vision settings, three-seed curves are shown for selected candidates, and conventional regularized/margin losses are added as comparators.
assumptions: A prototype's geometric proximity is assumed to be intrinsically interpretable, even when no class-level semantic or causal faithfulness test is performed.
High top-PC explained variance and fewer PCA dimensions are assumed to mean interpretability rather than collapse or loss of useful diversity.
Swapping the output head while retaining backbone recipes is assumed to isolate geometry despite metric-specific conditioning, temperature, exponent, and numerical-stability needs.

The intended HarMax inverse-distance link and the appendix's softmax-over-negative-distance implementation are assumed equivalent enough for conclusions to transfer, although mathematically they are not equivalent.
The shared n=1 and epsilon=1e-4 settings are assumed fair across dimensions and metrics, despite the original harmonic paper motivating an exponent near sqrt(d) for language models.
CodeCarbon readings from the reported hardware/location are assumed sufficiently stable for small per-run differences and transferable as sustainability evidence.
Per-step carbon overhead is assumed capable of being offset by faster convergence, although energy-to-target is not numerically demonstrated for language models.
The 10,000-iteration OpenWebText pretraining horizon is assumed sufficient to compare optimization and representation geometry of 0.1B-2B models.
Raw p<0.05 labels are treated as meaningful across many distance/metric comparisons even though the displayed adjusted p-values do not pass 0.05.
Joint scale invariance of representations and prototypes is assumed to control prototype norms in the stated fixed-representation theorem.
Accuracy and emissions from selected top configurations are assumed representative of a distance family despite strong backbone and dataset interactions.
A final classifier cost of O(Cd) or O(Vd) is assumed negligible relative to the backbone, including for large-vocabulary Qwen and covariance-based distances.

techniques.role: Provides a registry-based prototype classifier over multiple Euclidean, angular, normalized, discrete-relaxed, and covariance-aware geometries.
Treats each class or vocabulary column as a learned prototype and substitutes the normal linear output projection.
Jointly measures task quality, PCA/covariance structure, and CodeCarbon time/energy/emissions.
Normalizes stepwise gradient-norm variance against cross-entropy to summarize optimization volatility.
Uses entropy of the activation covariance spectrum to detect low-dimensional concentration or collapse.
Aggregates paired metric differences over 16 vision dataset-backbone settings, with both raw and adjusted p-values reported.
Retrains selected vision candidates for three seeds and plots mean accuracy trajectories with 95% intervals.
Tests delayed generalization and circular representation recovery under multiple distance heads.
Compares focal loss, label smoothing, center loss, confidence penalty, and ArcFace against harmonic heads.
Separates the nominal O(Cd) classifier cost from the much larger vision backbone FLOP budget.

limitations: Author-stated: non-Euclidean losses do not uniformly dominate Euclidean harmonic loss in accuracy, and positive aggregate accuracy medians for cosine/normalized Bray-Curtis are not statistically significant.

Author-stated: sustainability is architecture dependent; PVT often pays an emissions premium, covariance-aware and high-order metrics can be expensive, and energy-to-target should accompany per-step measurements.
Author-stated: Mahalanobis is sensitive to ill-conditioned covariance statistics and becomes unattractive for large-scale pretraining.
Author-stated: PCA is only a first-pass interpretability tool under approximately linear feature-superposition assumptions.
Reviewer-identified: the paper alternates between inverse-distance HarMax probabilities and ordinary softmax over negative distance, objectives with different gradients, scale properties, and optima.
Reviewer-identified: all adjusted p-values in Tables 9-11 exceed 0.05, but the 'Sig.' column and prose emphasize unadjusted tests across many comparisons.

Reviewer-identified: Table 10's caption says negative PCA@90 differences are improvements, while its prose interprets positive medians as improvements; the claimed direction cannot be recovered consistently.
Reviewer-identified: concentration in one or a few PCs is not validated as human interpretability and can be collapse; several highly concentrated heads have much worse accuracy.
Reviewer-identified: language radar plots omit absolute values, and no multi-seed numerical perplexity/stability/emissions table supports the broad language claims.
Reviewer-identified: Appendix L.3 reports higher per-1k-step emissions for every tested distance, contradicting claims of greener language heads absent a measured reduction in steps-to-target.
Reviewer-identified: Figure 7's aggregation totals and sign interpretation conflict across pages 43-44 and with Table 11, making aggregate emissions claims unreliable without raw-run reconstruction.

Reviewer-identified: only three seeds are shown for selected vision curves, the interval construction is unspecified, and selection of 'top-performing' candidates before retraining can bias uncertainty summaries.
Reviewer-identified: the stated five datasets times four backbones suggest 20 settings, but the Wilcoxon tables use 16 pairs without identifying omitted combinations.

Reviewer-identified: the shared n=1 setting differs sharply from the original harmonic paper's language-model heuristic n approximately sqrt(d), while distance-specific temperature/scale tuning is limited.

Reviewer-identified: Theorem A.2 uses joint scaling of fixed data and prototypes to justify compactness in W alone, and the PAC-Bayes section omits the objects and derivation required for a formal PAC-Bayes bound.

Reviewer-identified: the inverse-distance objective is singular at zero distance, so the claimed attained finite zero-distance optimum depends on an epsilon-clamped implementation not included in the theorem.
Reviewer-identified: 10,000 OpenWebText iterations are a short pretraining horizon for 0.5B-2B models and no downstream or long-horizon generalization evaluation is reported.

Reviewer-identified: large-vocabulary distance heads, especially Qwen's 151,936 prototypes and Mahalanobis variants, may not be negligible in memory traffic even when asymptotic backbone FLOPs dominate.
Reviewer-identified: the paper's anonymous code link and absence of raw CodeCarbon/run-selection tables make the internal emissions contradictions difficult to resolve independently.
failure_modes: A distance appears interpretable by collapsing representations into very few PCs while losing discriminative information and accuracy.
A metric wins on ResNet but fails on MLP, CNN, PVT, a harder dataset, or a different input resolution because conditioning and backbone geometry interact.
Softmax(-distance) is mistakenly analyzed as inverse-distance HarMax, invalidating the claimed scale-invariance and finite-minimizer mechanism.
Cosine distance approaches zero for correct prototypes, causing log/inverse-distance numerical singularities unless epsilon and temperature are carefully controlled.
Mahalanobis covariance estimates become singular, noisy, or memory-bound in high-dimensional and large-vocabulary settings.
Hamming relaxations optimize a continuous proxy that does not preserve hard binary distance behavior at inference.
Small CodeCarbon differences reflect run duration, grid search, early stopping, location, or utilization noise rather than intrinsic loss efficiency.
Per-step emissions rise and expected convergence savings never materialize, producing a larger end-to-end footprint despite smoother curves.
Selecting best variants on the same runs used for comparison produces winner's-curse accuracy and confidence intervals.
Raw p-values generate apparent discoveries that disappear after correction for the large metric-by-distance comparison family.
Prototype/vocabulary distance computation adds prohibitive bandwidth or kernel overhead even when its nominal FLOP fraction is small.
A one-size-fits-all exponent and no post-hoc scaling place some distances in flat or saturated gradient regimes.
Circular PCA geometry on modulo addition is treated as causal interpretability without testing whether the representation supports stable interventions or extrapolation.
A finite prototype norm coexists with unbounded backbone feature norms, so the purported norm-control benefit moves upstream rather than disappears.
reusable_insights: Treat the probability link and the distance metric as separate experimental factors; softmax(-d), softmax(-log d), and normalized d^-n are not interchangeable.
Report energy per step, wall-clock energy to a fixed target, and full-run cumulative energy separately; head FLOPs alone cannot establish sustainability.
Use task utility, collapse diagnostics, causal interventions, and human/semantic validation alongside PCA concentration before calling a representation interpretable.
Pre-register a metric-by-backbone grid and report multiplicity-corrected inference rather than selecting winners from radar plots.
Preserve configuration-level Pareto fronts: cosine is compelling on CIFAR ResNet even though the family-level dominance claim fails.
Match each distance's temperature/exponent while also providing a shared-hyperparameter control, because geometry and scale jointly determine gradients.
Use conventional angular/proxy losses such as ArcFace, AdaCos, and ProxyNCA-style heads as direct controls for any cosine prototype claim.
Test whether a prototype is a faithful class exemplar by nearest-example retrieval, counterfactual movement, calibration, and out-of-distribution behavior—not just proximity plots.
Audit theorem-to-code equivalence explicitly, including epsilon clamps and singular points, before attributing empirical behavior to formal properties.
Report all negative architecture/dataset cases prominently; they are useful routing evidence for practitioners choosing a geometry.
open_questions: Which objective was actually used in each run: inverse-distance HarMax, log-distance logits, or negative-distance softmax?
Do cosine's CIFAR ResNet gains survive parameter-, FLOP-, temperature-, augmentation-, and hyperparameter-budget-matched ArcFace/AdaCos/ProxyNCA comparisons?
Can the raw emissions logs reconcile the 650.49 g, 181.2 g, 16-pair, and 680-run aggregation descriptions and the Figure 7 sign reversal?
Does any language distance head reduce total energy to a fixed validation perplexity once its higher per-step emissions are counted?
Do the language perplexity and stability effects persist at compute-optimal token budgets and on downstream tasks?
Are low PCA dimensions predictive of concept-level faithfulness, intervention success, robustness, or merely collapse?
How should n or temperature scale with hidden dimension, vocabulary size, and the concentration profile of each distance?
Can a corrected finite-minimizer theorem be stated for end-to-end learned representations with epsilon-regularized inverse distances?
What PAC-Bayes prior/posterior and capacity norm yield the displayed bound, and is the bound numerically nonvacuous?
Why are only 16 of the nominal 20 vision dataset-backbone combinations used in aggregate tests?
How robust are the results to more seeds, independent selection/evaluation splits, and equal hyperparameter-search budgets?
Can covariance-aware distances be made vocabulary-scalable with diagonal, low-rank, or shared whitening without losing their claimed geometry?
Do the modulo-addition circles persist under different train fractions, moduli, initialization distributions, and representation-matched baselines?

competitive_landscape.title: Harmonic Loss Trains Interpretable AI Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Baek et al. introduce Euclidean HarMax probabilities, finite-distance prototypes, grokking/data-efficiency experiments, and GPT-2 representation geometry. The present paper's real extension is the metric sweep plus sustainability audit; however, its n=1 choice and negative-distance-softmax implementation description depart from the predecessor's explicit inverse-distance link and n approximately sqrt(d) language setting.

competitive_landscape.title: ProxyNCA++: Revisiting and Revitalizing Proxy Neighborhood Component Analysis
competitive_landscape.difference: ProxyNCA++ also learns class proxies and optimizes normalized sample-to-proxy distances, but uses exponentiated negative squared Euclidean distance, a tuned temperature, fast proxy learning rates, class-balanced sampling, and retrieval evaluation. It shows that link temperature and proxy optimization can dominate metric-head results—factors the harmonic study largely holds fixed—while not addressing HarMax, language modeling, or carbon reporting.
competitive_landscape.source_version: arXiv v2 / ECCV 2020 preprint; submitted 2020-04-02; last revised/source_date=2020-07-23

competitive_landscape.title: ArcFace: Additive Angular Margin Loss for Deep Face Recognition
competitive_landscape.difference: ArcFace normalizes features and class weights and adds an explicit geodesic angular margin, giving a precise hyperspherical interpretation with negligible stated overhead. The present cosine harmonic head uses distance-tailored probabilities without an explicit class margin and broadens to general vision/LLM tasks and emissions; its own alternative-loss tables show ArcFace can match or beat harmonic variants in several settings.
competitive_landscape.source_version: arXiv v4 / TPAMI version; submitted 2018-01-23; last revised/source_date=2022-09-04

competitive_landscape.title: Deep Simplex Classifier for Maximizing the Margin in Both Euclidean and Angular Spaces
competitive_landscape.difference: Deep Simplex Classifier jointly maximizes Euclidean and angular margins and fixes class centers to regular-simplex vertices on a hypersphere, targeting compact, interpretable, open-set decision regions without user-set margin parameters. The harmonic paper instead learns unconstrained prototypes, chooses one distance at a time, and emphasizes the heavy-tailed link and sustainability rather than coupled margins or open-set recognition.

competitive_landscape.title: Provably Adversarially Robust Nearest Prototype Classifiers
competitive_landscape.difference: Voracek and Hein analyze nearest-prototype decisions under distinct Lp decision and Lq threat metrics and provide scalable exact/lower-bound robustness certificates. The harmonic paper evaluates many distances and an informal margin/PAC-Bayes story, but offers no adversarial certificate or robustness evaluation; conversely PNPC does not use inverse-distance probabilities or study language/sustainability.
competitive_landscape.source_version: ICML 2022 PMLR volume 162 version of record; publication_date/source_date=2022-07-17

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The authors claim the first systematic extension of Euclidean harmonic loss to a wide family of non-Euclidean distances across vision and language models, the first controlled sustainability assessment of those heads, and an integrated accuracy-interpretability-carbon selection framework with preliminary metric-general theory.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The paper does contain an unusually broad head registry, five vision datasets, four backbones, four language-model configurations, CodeCarbon logging, conventional-loss comparisons, grokking plots, and extensive appendices. Cosine's CIFAR ResNet results are quantitatively strong, and the negative architecture-specific cases demonstrate that metric choice matters. Yet learned proxy classifiers, angular/cosine softmax losses, fixed-simplex prototype heads, distance-sensitive nearest-prototype theory, and the Euclidean HarMax mechanism all predate this work.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The defensible novelty is a broad empirical metric sweep inside the specific harmonic-head framing plus an attempt to put carbon accounting beside task and geometry metrics. Claims of general cosine dominance, improved interpretability, greener language training, and formal generalization are not established: objective definitions conflict, adjusted tests are null, PCA directionality is inconsistent, LLM results lack absolute tables, and every tested LLM distance has higher per-step emissions. Treat the work as a configuration atlas and hypothesis generator, with CIFAR ResNet cosine as a credible positive result, rather than a validated generally superior loss toolbox.

reviewer_notes: All 64 pages of the pinned extraction were read, including theory, architecture/configuration details, Wilcoxon tables, three-seed curves, every alternative-loss section, convergence plots, modulo-addition, FLOP accounting, geometry figures, per-setting vision tables, and language sustainability/interpretability appendices. PDF pages 30, 31, and 44 were inspected directly to verify table signs, adjusted p-values, and the Figure 7 emissions-axis contradiction. Five direct primary competitors were checked at current arXiv, CVF, and PMLR records on 2026-08-23, with exact current versions and source dates encoded in source_version. Negative/null results retained here include non-significant positive cosine/Bray-Curtis accuracy medians, no multiplicity-adjusted result below 0.05, poor CIFAR-100 CNN/MLP/PVT harmonic accuracy, large MarathiSign emissions premiums, qualitative rather than numeric LLM gains, and universally higher per-1k-step LLM emissions. The source pin exactly matches fulltext_index.jsonl. Confidence is high on the audit and extracted numbers, but lower on identifying the actual implemented probability link and on aggregate emissions because the paper itself is inconsistent.
